title: The mobile visit for a law practice
metaTitle: Law practice mobile website, first screen
excerpt: A law practice mobile website should show the matter you take and a way to request a consultation on the first phone screen. Desktop layout comes second.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it, a phone-sized plan sitting next to the desktop tools.
caption: Wireframes on a tablet, with the desktop keyboard waiting to one side. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on the first phone screen of a law firm site?
faqs.answer: The kind of matter you take, in the client's words, and a button to request a consultation. One supporting picture can sit with them if it does not push the sentence off the screen. Awards, Latin, and a long menu can wait below.

faqs.question: Why do desktop designs fail on a phone?
faqs.answer: A wide hero often stacks the photograph above the words, so the client sees texture before the matter. Hover menus and multi-column tables do not survive a thumb. Design the narrow screen first, then let the wide layout borrow from it.

faqs.question: How should a consultation form behave on a phone?
faqs.answer: Ask for the matter, a way to reply, and the deadline, with visible labels and keyboards that match the field. Keep the button large enough to tap without opening something else. The confirmation should say what happens next, and that the reply is not legal advice.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results
How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A law practice mobile website has to finish the job on the first screen of a phone. Show the kind of matter you take, and show a way to request a consultation. Do not let the desktop composition decide that screen. A client choosing counsel under time pressure is often between other tasks, on a small display, with a letter in the other hand.

W3C's overview of WCAG is explicit that the guidelines apply to mobile, not only to a wide monitor. Google's Core Web Vitals ask for Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint under 200 milliseconds, and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. Those thresholds are stricter in practice on a phone on an ordinary connection. A layout that only works when the window is wide fails the client you most need to help.

## Design the phone screen first

Start with a frame the width of a phone, and put only what the decision needs.

The matter, in the client's words, large enough to read without pinching. One example is enough in that first view. "We review shop leases before you sign." The other matters can follow as the page scrolls.

The consultation, as a real button with words. "Request a consultation." It should be visible without opening a menu. If a sticky bar carries it, the bar must not cover the matter sentence. A bar that hides the offer in order to advertise the offer is a mess.

One picture, cropped for the narrow frame. A face, a table, or the paper. Not a wide marble hall shrunk until it becomes a gray band. The picture supports the sentence. If it pushes the sentence below the fold, move the picture under the sentence.

Leave the founding year, the Latin motto, and the award row off that first screen. They can exist lower, if they are true and useful. They are not the sort.

Read the screen out loud. If you need a second scroll to learn what the firm takes and how to ask, the desktop layout has already won, and the client has already lost time.

## What the desktop file tends to break

Teams often design the wide page until it looks balanced, then stack the same blocks for the phone. The stack is innocent, and it still fails.

A hero that places the photograph on the left and the words on the right will usually stack the photograph first. The client then sees a texture, and the matter waits underneath. Put the words first in the document order, and let the wide layout move the picture beside them only when there is room.

A header with the logo, six jobs, a phone number, and a button will not fit. On a phone it collapses into a dense bar or a menu that hides the consultation. Keep the phone header to the name and the consultation. Put the jobs in a short menu, or let the page itself be the list, with links the thumb can hit.

Hover menus do not exist on a phone. If a service is only reachable by hovering "Practice areas," it is missing. Every job you want has to be a tap.

Type set for a desktop column often becomes a long gray paragraph on a phone, or a tiny caption under a full-bleed image. Set the matter at a size that reads at arm's length. Body text should be a normal reading size, with real line breaks, not a miniature of the print brochure.

Fixed elements deserve a count. A cookie banner, a chat bubble, a sticky header, and a sticky footer can together cover the matter and the button. Pick one persistent control, the consultation, and let the rest wait until the client has seen the offer.

## Touch, type, and the consultation

The consultation control has to be easy to tap. WCAG 2.2 includes a minimum target size of 24 by 24 CSS pixels for pointer inputs, with some spacing exceptions. Treat that as a floor, not a goal. A primary button should be larger, with space around it so a moving thumb does not open the menu instead.

The form, if it starts on this page, should ask for the kind of matter, a way to reply, and the deadline. Use an email keyboard for the email field and a telephone keyboard for the phone field. Label every field in text, not only with a placeholder that disappears. WCAG's principles, perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust, show up here as labels a person can see and a form a person can finish.

Do not ask for the life story, the opposing party's full address, and how they heard about you before you have said you can help. Those questions can come after a human replies. A long form on a phone is a resignation letter the client writes to themselves.

If some matters are emergencies, give them a separate control with the hours. Do not make every lease review compete with a red phone icon. Ordinary clients need a calm button. Urgent clients need a path that is actually staffed.

After they submit, the screen should say what happens next, in the same view. Who reads it. That the reply is about fit, not legal advice. What to do if the deadline is inside two days. A spinner and then silence feels like a failed send.

## Speed and stability on a real connection

Test on a phone, on a network you did not optimize for the office. The hero text and the button should be readable while images finish. If the only version of the matter line is burned into a giant image, the client waits for the picture before they can read. Put the words in text. Let the image be the image.

Keep LCP inside 2.5 seconds by shipping a photograph at the size the phone displays. A desktop original is a tax. Give the image its dimensions so the button does not jump down the page when the file arrives. That jump is a layout shift, and Google asks you to keep CLS under 0.1.

Keep the page quiet under the finger. A menu that stutters, a chat widget that loads late and shoves the button, or a script that waits on a map of every office will blow the 200 millisecond INP budget. Maps can wait on the contact page, and only if location is something the client must see before they request time.

Reduced motion matters on this visit. If you animate the hero, provide a still version for people who have asked the system to reduce motion. A slow pan across stone makes some people leave for reasons that have nothing to do with your skill. The matter sentence does not need to move.

Cache and versions still count. When you replace the hero, change the file name or the asset version so the phone does not keep last year's marble frame beside this year's sentence.

## A review you can do in the hallway

You do not need a lab. Use a phone and one person who did not design the page.

1. Load the homepage on a cellular connection, or on the office Wi-Fi with the phone in your hand, not mirrored on a monitor.
2. Without scrolling, read what matter the firm takes and find the consultation.
3. Tap the consultation. Fill it with a thumb, including one mistake, and see if you can fix the mistake without zooming.
4. Rotate nothing clever. Just go back and open the shop-lease job from the menu. Confirm the heading matches the label you tapped.
5. Scroll the first service. The outcome and the boundary should be readable. The button should not sit under a sticky bar.

If step 2 fails, change the order of the first screen before you debate the typeface. If step 3 fails, shorten the form. If the menu and the heading disagree, fix the words. Nielsen Norman Group's finding that people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds is the reason step 2 comes first. The rest of the site is for the client who stayed.

Do this again after any visual polish. Decoration has a habit of growing back into the first screen once the desktop file looks empty without it.

## Pages that must survive the same test

The homepage is the usual failure, and it is not the only one. The pricing page, the services page, and the contact page are often opened from a search result straight onto a phone. Each of them still needs the matter, or the fee shape, and a consultation the thumb can hit.

A pricing page that is a wide table will collapse into an unreadable smear. Restack it as a heading, a shape, and two short lists per matter. A services page that depended on three columns should become a sequence of blocks with the outcome first. An about page of tiny headshots in a grid should become names and matters, with faces large enough to recognize.

The contact page is where the phone visit either finishes or dies. It should tell them what happens after they reach out, how fast, and what to have ready. A map of the car park is optional. The reply path is not.

## When the desktop and the phone disagree

If the partnership reviews the site on a laptop in a conference room, they will approve a composition the client never sees. Ask them to review on their own phones, in the room, with the brightness down. The comments will change. The marble will look smaller. The button will look either obvious or missing. Believe the phone.

You can keep a beautiful wide layout. It is the second version. The phone version is the one that has to show the kind of matter and the way to request a consultation without a scroll, or with as little scroll as the photograph truly requires. Build that one, then let the wide page borrow from it.

Once the first screen works, the contact path is the next place a mobile client stalls. Read [what the contact page has to explain](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-law-practice) before you add fields that made sense on a paper intake sheet.

When you want a second opinion on a first screen that has to work on a phone, [book an intro call with Hanabi](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the page on your own device, not a slide of the desktop.
